title: How do we bisect four angles of different sizes?
description: A question from the book asks for at least four different angles and their bisectors. Four angles of clearly different sizes are drawn and each is bisected in the same way as the example in the book, with the triangle pair checked each time.
teaching_notes: One idea: the same steps bisect an angle of any size, because equal marks on the arms and equal arcs always give two triangles with three pairs of equal sides. Watch for students who make the arcs too short for an obtuse angle.

video_script.why: The child has bisected one angle and has not yet seen that the same steps work for small, large and obtuse angles.
video_script.substitution: Each angle is bisected in the same way as the example in the book: equal marks on the arms, equal arcs from them, and a join to the vertex.
video_script.anchor: Construct at least four different angles, and draw their bisectors.
video_script.payoff_line: Each bisector is the line O C

final_answer.value: Each bisector is OC, where OA = OB and AC = BC; ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS, so the two halves are equal
final_answer.spoken: each bisector is the line O C, where O eigh equals O B and eigh C equals B C, so the two halves are equal

never_show: the bisector OC before step four
maths_rules: Four angles of clearly different sizes: a small acute angle, a right angle made with equal arcs, a large acute angle and an obtuse angle.
For each angle with vertex O: an arc with centre O cuts the arms at A and B, so OA = OB.
Equal arcs from A and from B, long enough to meet, meet at C inside the angle: AC = BC.
Triangle OAC is congruent to triangle OBC by SSS (OA = OB, AC = BC, OC common), so angle AOC = angle BOC and OC is the bisector.
video_script.design: One idea: the same four moves bisect any angle. The check is the triangle pair, as in the book's example.

<bookmark mark='m3'/>The two angles at O are equal, so the two halves are equal in every angle.
